title: Early-disconnect grace period, ephemeral-buffer drain, and abort GC strategies
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Some long-running generations are left in limbo when clients disconnect abruptly or network flaps, causing memory pressure on serving nodes and partial/duplicate outputs when clients reconnect. Existing heuristics are tuned for epoch fencing and lease windows but we observe tail cases under low-traffic, high-concurrency workloads where ephemeral buffers accumulate and cold-started reconnects re-trigger expensive KV prefix delivery.

Goal: Design and implement a graceful early-disconnect strategy with a configurable grace period + staggered ephemeral-buffer drain that balances user experience (fast resume when appropriate) against resource reclamation and correctness for structured outputs/tool calls. The feature should: 1) allow short transient disconnects to resume without full regen, 2) ensure partial generations that will never be resumed are garbage-collected quickly, 3) avoid duplicate tool/function invocations on resume, 4) expose controls for Dedicated/Private tenants to tune retention windows.

Success criteria: 
- Reduce average ephemeral-buffer retention per node by >= 40% in our benchmark scenario (10k concurrent streams, 60s median gen length)
- No increase in duplicate tool invocations in canary tests (0 observed duplicates across 1k resumes)
- Resume latency for transient reconnects within 150ms of baseline 95th percentile
- Configurable knobs surfaced in Console and default safe policy applied to Hosted clusters.

Design notes and constraints:
- Introduce a two-stage state for disconnected sessions: SOFT_PENDING (grace period where KV cache and output fragments are retained and resumable) and HARD_PENDING (accelerated GC window where we keep minimal metadata to allow idempotent verification but reclaim bulk memory).
- Use a monotonic disconnect-counter + resume-token signed with ephemeral key to prevent replays that would re-run tool calls. Resume-token includes last-ack-offset to allow structured output reconciliation without re-executing side effects.
- On transition to HARD_PENDING, compact prefix caches aggressively (keep only markers needed to reconstruct structured outputs up to last safe token) and demote large ephemeral blobs to eviction queue with backpressure-aware pacing.
- For function/tool-calls: require durable invocation marker in the lineage before allowing resume to avoid double-invoke; if missing, resume should replay only idempotent tool calls or return explicit conflict state to client to surface manual reconciliation.
- Console/tenant knobs: grace_period_seconds, hard_pending_seconds, max_ephemeral_bytes_per_session, allow_resume_tool_calls (enum: always, idempotent-only, never). Hosted defaults to 45s soften / 5m hard; Dedicated customers can lower to optimize cost.

Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (proto): server-side state transition + in-memory soft/hard states, resume token shape, basic GC worker (2 wks)
- Phase 2 (safety): integration with tool-call lineage and idempotency markers, tests to block duplicate side effects (2 wks)
- Phase 3 (hardening): eviction pacing, metrics, Console feature flag and config UI, canary rollout (2 wks)

Risks and trade-offs:
- Keeping longer grace periods improves UX but increases memory pressure; default must target typical PLG usage, not enterprise heavy gen workloads.
- Strict idempotency requirements may force clients to adopt more structured tool APIs; we will provide fallback conflict responses to minimize breakage.
- Resume-token signing introduces short-lived keys; key rollover and clock skew must be handled (use server epoch + tolerant verification window).
